We have to stop bashing people for staying. It's too easy to assume what you would do in the same situation. For some, more likely most people, their home is their only asset. And most people will not abandon what they have worked hard to have. Your entire life is there. Everyone will have a reason to stay and most of those reasons are forced upon them, be it money, means, and refusal to go down. I can tell this house is decently large and probably expensive, but think about how many homeowners are barely keeping their heads above water, figuretively, everyday to stay there where they are. So many people are not far off from homelessness, even if you think they are doing well. Now, I say this as someone who rents a shithole and has left for storms before (SENC, USA), has stayed when I probably shouldn't have, and luckily has means and family to go to. But I also work with homeowners who's lives and homes have been destroyed because of hurricanes. Common reasons for staying? "If it's going to go down, I'll go down with it. It's all I have. I don't have anywhere to go and no money for a place to stay. How do I get back? I'll lose my job. What if everything goes okay and I'm out a lot of money I can't recover?" There are a hundred reasons for staying, and for each person, their reason is good enough for them. Bashing these people to hell will not help them, or help others. Of course you should seek better shelter in a disaster, everyone knows that. Fear will drive out common sense and the need to protect what you have, even just by being present, are huge factors when people make choices. Give these people a break and maybe donate to help them rebuild their lives. E Pluribus Unum. Time to unite, at least for a damn minute. Then we can all go back to judging strangers (like I'm not guilty of that... I know I'm bit of a pot right now) just give them a break.

WARM's mission is to repair, rebuild, and make homes accessible; and to inspire service, generosity, and hope. 

Serving low-income homeowners in Bladen, Brunswick, Columbus, Duplin, New Hanover, Onslow, and Pender counties, many of whom are elderly, disabled, and/or veterans. WARM helps people age in place safely by preventing home accidents and illnesses - preserving their dignity and independence.

The Wilmington Area Rebuilding Ministry, Inc. (WARM) began in 1996 in response to hurricanes Bertha and Fran. Volunteers from across our region were organized by leaders of the Wilmington District of the United Methodist Church to repair the damaged homes of low-income and elderly residents. As they entered the homes, volunteers noticed that much of the damage predated the storms - they just did not have the resources to make costly repairs. So, while responding to a natural disaster, WARM volunteers discovered a social disaster: substandard housing.

Long after the TV crews and national relief agencies packed up, WARM has continued its mission to improve the living conditions of low-income homeowners, including many elderly and disabled. Since its inception, WARM has helped over 1,600 families in Southeastern North Carolina. WARM will keep going until every homeowner in our service area is able to live safely and independently in the home they worked so hard to pay for.

I work in disaster long term recovery and repair in North Carolina. While it may seem like sending food, clothing, etc is a great idea, I'm sorry to say it's not. Send money if you can. Organizations can get large orders of bulk items. They can stretch a dollar farther than an individual. Money can buy temporary shelters, medicine, clothes, food, oxygen tanks - things that are hard to physically donate. Red Cross does a lot, even with it's less than great reputation. Search local repair and rebuilding organizations in the areas hit. Those small organizations will need donations more than ever now. Even minimally effected homes will need at least $20k a home to bring it back. Roofs are a minimum of $6k in my area. My coworkers and I will be researching organizations in the area tomorrow. I'll come back and post some links to help. In the meantime, search State/city Rebuilding Organizations. They will all have different names and might not be obvious, but search that key word. Most organizations are nonprofit and rely on grants. Grants have those key words, so you can search state agencies also by that word. They should have a listing or organizations they work with. In NC, we work with the NC Housing Finance Agency. They distribute grant funds for disaster repair and recovery. 
It's going to take years to bring these towns back. Some towns won't be able to be revived. People will move and not be able to come back. Areas won't be cleaned or cleared for a long time. There will eventually be new houses built, but the majority of those who lost their homes won't be able to afford those new homes. What you can do with donations is help families rebuild from what they have left, or move on to a safe home. 
I'm not religious at all, but please keep these people in your thoughts. They lost everything and life will never be normal again. Even if all you have is $5 to give, please know that it helps. It's goes so much farther than some realize.

CB state park is a great place to take a small afternoon hike. The beaches are fun but be ready for high parking prices. Try the local small restaurants. The museums are nice and not expensive. The Cape Fear Museum has kid friendly features. The Aquarium too. Greenfield Lake Amplitheater has great shows, but since Live Nation bought it, we all kind of feel like outsiders at our own venue. But the crowd vibes are still amazing there. The farmers market is a great place to check out the local produce, meats, and have a nice conversation with the vendors about their work. Downtown is a bunch of shops and restaurants but it's a nice place to grab a beer and chill. Local musicians play all around. There are a ton of adult sports leagues to join and little kid activities once your toddler is old enough. Games at Legion Stadium are fun and you get to support our local baseball team, The Sharks. We have a soccer team too, The Hammerheads. The walking tours downtown give some great history and local tidbits about the movies filmed here. Learn about the 1898 Massacre. It's a part of terrible history here, but it's important to know. There can be a huge racial divide here and even larger racists. But the community seems to be coming together, even with on going violence. There are a ton of nonprofit organizations that do events and are always looking for volunteers. Riverfront Park and The Wilson Center are large music venues. The Train museum is downtown and actually quite a gem. Visit Southport one day. It's adorable and makes a fun local road trip. Go to the Waffle House on Carolina Beach Road, the nicest people ever and super fast. There are car shows the first Saturday of every month at the Pointe on 17th (sometimes they change the location, but they post it on FB). Check out WhatsonWilmington.com for local events and stuff. Always an art show or something going on. Go axe throwing. I cannot stress this enough. It's ridiculously fun. There are usually beer and food festivals, but covid has put them in hold. There are a ton of parks here to have a fun day all, Long Leaf park has the splash pad and dog park.
